text: Isaac Sorious is known for a series of thirteen etchings showing the destruction caused by French troops in the province of Utrecht in the Disaster Year 1672. He also made satirical allegorical prints, for instance on the subject of the stadtholder William III of Orange. Nothing is known about his birth or death, and he is recorded only between 1672 and 1676. In those years he worked in Utrecht and Amsterdam, and possibly in Rome. He was a Dutch engraver, etcher and painter.

Joseph Karl Stieler painted the Gallery of Beauties at Nymphenburg Palace and one of the best-known portraits of Beethoven. From 1820 to 1855 he was royal court painter to the Bavarian kings. He was born in Mainz into a long-established family of engravers, punchcutters and die makers, and his father, August Friedrich, gave him some artistic training. After his father's early death Stieler completed his apprenticeship on his own and began as a painter of miniatures, which the middle classes increasingly sought. When French revolutionary troops occupied Mainz in 1792, he followed the expelled court to Aschaffenburg.

Manuel Orazi created the Calendrier Magique in 1895, an occult-themed calendar still noted for its graphic design. He limited it to 777 copies and worked on it with the popular French author Austin de Croze, who wrote the text. Orazi was an Italian Art Nouveau illustrator, poster artist and jewelry designer, and a set creator for theater and film. Not much is known about him, and his background is obscure. He was born in Rome in 1860. Sympathetic to the French Decadent movement and Symbolism, he also made illustrations and typographic ornaments for books.

Norbert Goeneutte's father found him a place in an attorney's office, but Norbert persuaded his mother that he was not suited to the work. He entered the École des Beaux-arts and studied with Isidore Pils. When Pils died in 1875, Henri Lehmann replaced him, and the students disliked Lehmann so much that they wrote to Édouard Manet asking him to take over. Manet declined, and Goeneutte left to set up his own studio. He frequented the cabaret Père Lathuille, where he met Manet. He also illustrated a novel by Émile Zola.

Adrien Barrère's poster of caricatures of the Paris Medical Faculty was so popular that no medical student left without a copy, and 420,000 were printed. The original, held at the University of Rouen, is twice the size of the later copies. Born Adrien Baneux in Paris, he studied law and medicine before turning to illustration and caricature. He designed a large number of posters for Parisian cinemas and the Grand Guignol. His work for Pathé was particularly successful, and in 1912 a trade journal called him Pathé's man of the hour and designer of more than two hundred posters.

Dick Ket was born with a serious heart defect, and debilitating weakness and phobias kept him from travelling. After 1930 he lived secluded in his parents' house in Bennekom. He saw modern art mainly through reproductions and concentrated on still lifes and self-portraits. His earliest paintings are impressionistic, but in 1929 the Neue Sachlichkeit decisively influenced him, and he went on to paint in a style he called New Realism, which has affinities with magic realism. His health worsened in his last decade, and he died young in 1940.

Art historian Tutta Palin called Ester Helenius a worshipper of ecstasy because of her strong use of colour. Helenius was a Finnish artist, mainly a painter but also trained in printmaking. She was an artist in residence at the Lallukka Artists' Home in Helsinki, and her work from that period was shown at the Helsinki Art Museum in 2020 and 2021. Palin's book on her, Ester Helenius: Värihurmion palvoja, brought her new attention after her death. Her sales records have been donated to the Hämeenlinna Art Museum.

Jacques Fabien Gautier d'Agoty made anatomical plates in colour with the physician Guichard Joseph Duverney, among them the Myologie complète en couleur et grandeur naturelle. Born in Marseille, he began as a pupil of Jacob Christoph Le Blon, the inventor of colour printing with blue, yellow and red. He claimed that Le Blon rebuffed his idea for an improved method using black. Later he and his sons spread colour engraving in France and published an illustrated journal for many years. The Académie of Dijon elected him a member.

Qiu Ying began as a lacquer artisan, painting decorations on lacquerware, after his peasant family moved from Taicang to Suzhou. Despite his humble origins he had natural talent and later learned painting from Zhou Chen. Suzhou's Wu School encouraged ink washes, but Qiu Ying also painted in the blue-and-green style. He mixed techniques freely. His figure, landscape and flower paintings all have a quality of originality. He specialised in the gongbi brush technique and is regarded as one of the Four Masters of the Ming dynasty.

Paolo Farinati's first major work was an altarpiece for the Duomo of Mantua. He was a Mannerist painter active mainly in his native Verona, but also in Mantua and Venice, and a contemporary of Paolo Veronese. According to Vasari, his father taught him first, and he was probably taught by Antonio Badile as well. He formed his initial style partly on the influence of Giulio Romano in Mantua. The chapel of the Sacrament in the same church was frescoed at the same time by Farinati, Veronese, Domenico Riccio and Battista del Moro.

Jan Hackaert sketched miners at work in the mountains, and more than once the workers, who could not understand what he was doing, thought he was a spy or was hexing them and complained. He travelled in Germany and Switzerland and mostly painted and sketched landscapes. Because Italianate landscapes were so fashionable, his Lake Zurich was mistaken for an Italian lake for years. He also painted landscape backgrounds for other painters, such as Nicolaes Berchem and Adriaen van de Velde.

John Neagle began with instruction from the drawing-master Pietro Ancora and an apprenticeship to Thomas Wilson, a painter of signs and coaches in Philadelphia. Wilson introduced him to Bass Otis and Thomas Sully, and Neagle became Sully's protégé. In 1818 he decided to concentrate exclusively on portraits. He married Sully's stepdaughter Mary in 1826, and for a time the son-in-law and father-in-law dominated portraiture in the city. Apart from brief stays in Lexington and New Orleans, he spent his career in Philadelphia, where he also directed the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.

Joseph Alanen produced over a hundred works depicting scenes from the Kalevala. He had trained as an electrician at an industrial school in Tampere, but he studied drawing, painting and anatomy and continued his art studies in Stockholm. He also studied in Berlin and Dresden between 1906 and 1910, where his teachers included Hans Dahl and Lovis Corinth. During the Finnish Civil War he supported the White Guard and illustrated postcards meant to promote Finnish nationalism. He died of the Spanish flu in 1920.

Sofonisba Anguissola's apprenticeship with local painters set a precedent for women to be accepted as students of art. She was born in Cremona to a relatively poor noble family and received a well-rounded education. In Rome she was introduced to Michelangelo, who recognised her talent, and in Milan she painted the Duke of Alba. The Spanish queen, Elizabeth of Valois, was a keen amateur painter, and in 1559 Anguissola went to Madrid as her tutor, with the rank of lady-in-waiting. After the queen's death, King Philip helped arrange an aristocratic marriage for her.

According to the RKD, Willem Romeyn was a pupil of Nicolaes Berchem in Haarlem in 1642. He became a member of the Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke in 1646 and later travelled to Rome. Back in Haarlem he served the guild as vinder in 1659. His landscapes often show grazing animals, particularly cattle and sheep, and these have been confused with the works of Berchem and others. Wilhelm von Kobell was his follower.

Bertha Wegmann became the first woman to hold a chair at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. Her family moved to Copenhagen when she was five, and her father, a merchant and art lover, spent much of his spare time painting. She received no formal education until she was nineteen and began lessons with Frederik Ferdinand Helsted and others. With her parents' support she then moved to Munich and lived there until 1881. She was not satisfied with studio teaching and decided to study directly from nature. She made friends with the Swedish painter Jeanna Bauck.

Francesco Londonio trained as a painter under Ferdinando Porta and Giovanni Battista Sassi in Milan, but he also travelled to Rome and Naples. He studied engraving with Benigno Bossi. He is best known for paintings and etchings of rustic and pastoral subjects, in which animals and peasants dominate the landscape. This focus on genre themes was popular among wealthy patrons, especially in northern Italy, and painters such as Ceruti and Cifrondi worked with similar themes. Londonio also did scenography, and a poorly conserved nativity scene on cut wooden shapes survives at the church of San Marco in Milan.

Hans Canon is a pseudonym. The man behind it, Johann Baptist Strašiřipka, was born in Vienna and began using the name after Slavic names became a handicap amid the separatist movements of the Empire, perhaps inspired by his service in the artillery. He seems to have been an indifferent student but showed an interest in art, so in 1845 he enrolled briefly at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and then studied privately with Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller and Carl Rahl. From 1847 to 1855 he served as an army officer.

Willem Arondéus took part in the bombing of the Amsterdam public records office, meant to hinder the German effort to identify Dutch Jews and others wanted by the Gestapo. He was caught and executed soon after his arrest, and Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations. Before the war he worked as an illustrator, designer of posters and wall hangings, and painter. In 1923 he was commissioned to paint a large mural for Rotterdam City Hall. He was openly gay and asserted it before his execution.

Abraham van den Tempel took his name from a house in Leiden with a relief of a temple in the keystone, where he lived as a student. He probably learned painting from his father, Lambert Jacobsz, who had taught Govert Flinck and Jacob Backer and died in 1636, the year Abraham moved to Amsterdam. He stayed there until 1647 and then moved to Leiden. He became a pupil of Jacob Backer and studied mathematics at Leiden University. The Leiden city council gave him several generous commissions, including three large allegorical paintings on the cloth industry.

Jan Boeckhorst became a canon in the Jesuit order at 17 and only started his artistic studies at about twenty-two. He was born in Münster as the second-oldest of twelve children, and his father Heinrich was for a while the mayor of the city. In the mid 1620s he moved to Antwerp, apparently to study with Rubens, although there is no firm evidence for that. He painted history pictures and genre scenes as well as portraits, in a style influenced by Rubens, Van Dyck and Jordaens. He also designed cartoons for weavers.

Joseph Coiny won the Prix de Rome in engraving in 1816. He was the son of the engraver Jacques Joseph Coiny, with whom he began his studies before becoming a pupil of François-Louis Gounod and Bervic. His works include The Creation of Eve, after Michelangelo, and numerous portraits. He was born in Paris in 1795 and died in his hometown in 1829. He was a French engraver.

Juan Correa de Vivar grew up wealthy in Mascaraque, in Castile. When he was 17 or 18 he joined the studio of Juan de Borgoña, where he met other Spanish artists and befriended Pedro de Cisneros. His nephew Rodrigo was apprenticed with him and continued some of his works after his death. In Mascaraque he was a substantial landowner with a nice house where he did much of his painting. He took frequent trips but always stayed in the Toledo area. When he died, he split his possessions between Rodrigo and the church of Mascaraque.

Lodewijk de Vadder was the first Flemish landscape painter to make dune landscapes the main feature of his pictures. His landscapes move away from the Mannerist tradition toward a more naturalistic approach, with looser brushwork and an emphasis on atmospheric effects. His loose handling shows the influence of Rubens and Adriaen Brouwer, while his restrained palette shows he knew what was happening in the Dutch Republic. He came from a family of painters, since his father and his brothers Philippe and Huybrecht were painters. He was also a draughtsman and an engraver.

Scarsellino's landscapes, on sacred and secular themes, strongly anticipate the landscape painting traditions of the 17th century. He was born and died in Ferrara, the son of the painter Sigismondo Scarsella, who was particularly skilled as an architect. He travelled and worked extensively across Italy. He lived in Venice for four years around 1570 and reportedly trained in the studio of Veronese. In Ferrara he worked alongside the Carracci brothers in the Palazzo dei Diamanti, and the Ferrarese and Bolognese painters influenced each other.

Anne Vallayer-Coster was admitted to the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture in 1770, at the age of twenty-six. Still life had low status at the time, but her highly developed skills, especially with flowers, soon drew the attention of collectors and other artists. Marie Antoinette took a particular interest in her paintings. Her life was private, dignified and hard-working. She survived the Reign of Terror, but the fall of the monarchy, her primary patrons, made her reputation decline. She also painted portraits and genre scenes.

Cristoforo Roncalli was one of the three painters known as Pomarancio. He was born in Pomarance, a small town near Volterra, to a well-to-do merchant family, and he first studied in Florence. By 1575 he had moved to Siena, where Ippolito Agostini commissioned him to paint an altarpiece for the cathedral and to fresco a ceiling in his palace with allegories from Ovid's Metamorphoses. Around 1578 he relocated to Rome, where the Compagnia di Santa Caterina commissioned two scenes from the Life of St. Catherine.

Jan Porcellis shifted marine painting toward overcast skies and rough waters, a radical break from the earlier focus on the grandeur of ships in historical settings. His works initiated a decisive transition from early realism to the tonal phase. Most of his canvases show sea and sky, which set the ground for later works in the genre. He was born in Ghent in the early 1580s, and in 1584 his parents joined Protestants fleeing the city. He married in Rotterdam in 1605, and his daughter was baptized in Middelburg in 1609.

Salomon de Bray was a Catholic, so he probably made altarpieces for Haarlem's underground Catholic churches, known as staties. He was born in Amsterdam and settled in Haarlem before 1617. He is registered as a pupil of Goltzius and Cornelis van Haarlem, though his training probably began in Amsterdam with Jan Pynas and Pieter Lastman. He painted history pieces, portraits and landscapes, and he also worked as an architect. He was a poet too, and his friend the composer Cornelis Padbrué set one of his poems to music.

Daniël Dupré was born in Amsterdam and lived and worked there for most of his life. He was an engraver and painter who also drew and worked in watercolour, and his paintings and prints depict mostly buildings and landscapes. He studied under Jurriaan Andriessen at the Stadstekenacademie, the city drawing school. He travelled around Germany and Italy, where he visited Düsseldorf, Rome and Mannheim. In the end he returned to Amsterdam.

Pedro Berruguete adopted Flemish techniques and conventions, which makes him part of the Hispano-Flemish style. He is most famous for paintings of the first years of the Inquisition and for religious imagery for Castilian retablos. Some consider him the first Renaissance painter in Spain. His son Alonso became the most important sculptor of the Spanish Renaissance, and because of Alonso's fame Pedro is sometimes called Berruguete the Elder. It is speculated that Pedro travelled to Italy around 1480 and worked at the court of Federico da Montefeltro in Urbino.

Jozef Božetech Klemens chose his middle name after an 11th-century painter and sculptor who was the last abbot of Sázava Monastery. He was born in Liptovský Mikuláš, the son of a saddler and carriage maker, and he first showed his artistic talent by painting pictures on his father's coaches. He became an assistant at a printing shop owned by a Slovak patriot, who promoted his education. In 1837 he was admitted to the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague for a trial period and then studied there for five years. After 1839 he also taught at a girls' school.

Matteo di Giovanni was born around 1430 in Borgo Sansepolcro, and his family moved to Siena, where he is firmly associated with the city's art. He married twice. His first wife, in 1463, was a wealthy noblewoman, and after her death he married a rich widow, who made it possible for him to buy real estate. Little is documented about his early career, and nothing is recorded about his apprenticeship. He may have trained in the workshop of Vecchietta, but he was clearly influenced by Sassetta and Domenico di Bartolo.

George Arnald is best known for his celebrated painting of the Battle of the Nile. He specialised in landscapes, including topographical views for illustrated county histories. Little is known about his early years, but he is believed to have begun his working life as a domestic servant before turning to the study of art. He was a student of the landscape painter and engraver William Pether. Arnald first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1788 and eventually had 176 works shown there, as well as 63 at the British Institution. The Royal Academy elected him an associate member in 1810.

Giovanni Battista Naldini began with a long apprenticeship in the studio of Jacopo Pontormo. In 1562 Giorgio Vasari recruited him, and he painted two crowded, mannerist canvases for the Studiolo of Francesco I in the Palazzo Vecchio, the Allegory of Dreams and the Gathering of Ambergris. He supplied altarpieces to Santa Maria Novella and Santa Croce, and he painted the Calling of Saint Matthew for the Salviati Chapel in San Marco alongside Francesco Morandini. Freedberg describes his work as distantly derived from Andrea del Sarto, through Pontormo and Vasari.

August Jerndorff was born in Oldenburg, the son of the court painter Just Ulrik Jerndorff. He trained first under Christian Hetsch, artistic director at the Royal Porcelain Factory, then attended the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts for five years and studied privately with Skovgaard. In 1875 he received the Academy's travel scholarship and lived in Italy for three years. He became acquainted with the latest Realist tendencies in European painting but remained relatively unaffected by them. In 1880 he co-founded a painting academy with Laurits Tuxen and Frans Schwartz. He is best known for his portraits.

Hendrik Gerrit ten Cate was an amateur entomologist as well as an artist. He was born and died in Amsterdam, where he worked from 1821 until his death at 53, leaving a widow and a large family. His pupils included Cornelis Springer and Adrianus Eversen. He worked in oil, ink and watercolour. His subjects included landscapes and winter scenes, cityscapes, portraits and, in his later years, moonlit cityscapes.

The fifth of six children of small farmers and linen weavers, Peter August Böckstiegel grew up in Werther. After showing artistic talent, he was apprenticed to a painter and glazier in Bielefeld. In 1907 he attended the new arts and crafts school. A 1909 visit to the Folkwang Museum in Essen first exposed him to the latest French painting trends. In 1913 a scholarship took him to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts, where he studied with Oskar Zwintscher and Otto Gussmann and became a lifelong friend of Conrad Felixmüller, whose sister Hanna later became his wife.

John White Abbott worked as a surgeon and apothecary in Exeter and painted as a keen amateur in watercolour and oils. He studied with Francis Towne, who was also his friend and whom he supported as a patron, and his watercolour style was based on Towne's. His work was primarily watercolour landscapes, for which he toured the Lake District, along with oil history paintings. He exhibited regularly at the Royal Academy between 1795 and 1805. After inheriting an estate at 62, he retired there and in 1831 became a deputy lieutenant of Devonshire.

Filippo Palizzi is known for rural genre scenes with animals, mostly goats. His brothers Francesco Paolo and Giuseppe also became painters. He was the fifth of thirteen children of a lawyer and an amateur musician. In 1836 he joined Giuseppe in Naples and the next year entered the Royal Institute of Fine Arts, where he soon fell out with his landscape professor, Gabriele Smargiassi, over art and politics. He withdrew to attend the private school of Giuseppe Bonolis. In 1839 he had his first showing, at the Academy, and the Duchess of Berry bought one of his works.

Viktor Vasnetsov was born in the remote village of Lopyal in Vyatka Governorate, the second of seven children. His father was a priest and a scholar of the natural sciences and astronomy, and his grandfather was an icon painter. Viktor and his brother Apollinary both became painters. In Lopyal Viktor started to paint, mostly landscapes and scenes of village life. He specialised in mythological and historical subjects and is considered a co-founder of Russian folklorist and romantic nationalistic painting.

Edgar Chahine's first painting shown at the Paris Salon was a portrait of a beggar. He was born in Vienna but moved to Constantinople very young, where his father, the director of the Ottoman Bank, paid for his studies. His teacher Melkon Tiratzuyan advised him to study in Italy, and in Venice he attended the Armenian Moorat-Raphael College and studied under Antonio Ermolao Paoletti at the Accademia. In 1895 he moved to Paris and enrolled at the Académie Julian. He worked there as a painter, engraver and illustrator of Armenian descent.

Jean-Pierre Houël lived through the reign of Louis XV, the French Revolution and Napoleon's First Empire. He was born in Rouen into a family of prosperous artisans, who sent him to the city's drawing academy at fifteen. There he saw early Dutch and Flemish painting, which had a defining impact on his landscapes. In 1758 he published a book of landscape engravings. His patrons then secured him a place at the French Academy in Rome, where he was captivated by Italian customs, landscapes and ancient sites and travelled throughout southern Italy making gouache drawings.

Baron László Mednyánszky spent most of his life moving around Europe as an artist, despite his aristocratic background. He spent considerable periods in seclusion but mingled with people across society, from the aristocracy and the army to the peasantry, and many of them became the subjects of his paintings. His most important works show scenes of nature and poor, working people, particularly from his home region in the Kingdom of Hungary. He was born in Beckov, now in Slovakia, and was also a philosopher. He is known too as a painter of Upper Hungarian and Slovak folklore.

Ambrosius Bosschaert the Elder is recognised as one of the earliest painters who made floral still lifes an independent genre. He was born in Antwerp, but he spent most of his career in Middelburg, where he moved with his family because of the threat of religious persecution. He signed his flower paintings with the monogram AB, the B set inside the A. At twenty-one he joined the city's Guild of Saint Luke, and he later became its dean. He founded a dynasty of painters who turned Middelburg into the leading centre for flower painting in the Dutch Republic.

Jean Raoux refused to paint portraits except in character. Born in Montpellier, he became a member of the Academy in 1717 as a historical painter. His reputation rested on decorations in a Venice palace, painted during three years in Italy, and on the Four Ages of Man, which the grand prior of Vendôme commissioned. His works are a long series of sets of the Seasons, the Hours and the Elements, or scenes of amusement and gallantry, in which his younger rival Watteau surpassed him. After a stay in England in 1720, he decorated rooms in the Temple.

Jacob Savery was born in Kortrijk into a family of painters. As Anabaptists, the Savery family left Flanders around 1580 for fear of Spanish persecution. They first stayed in Antwerp, where Savery was mentioned as the best student of the landscape painter Hans Bol. He settled around 1584 in Haarlem. There he married Trijntgen Kokelen in 1587, and the family then moved to Amsterdam, where he joined the Guild of St Luke. He painted and etched still lifes, animals and landscapes.

Isaac Cornelis Elink Sterk signed his work I.C. Elink Sterk. Born in Amsterdam, he settled in The Hague, where he took lessons from Cornelis Kruseman. Kruseman was a brother-in-law of his half-brother Augustus, and the two of them witnessed Kruseman's wedding in 1832. He mostly drew and painted portraits. He also made lithographs after artists such as Ary Scheffer, Aleida Budde and Jan Willem Pieneman.

Nicolas Bonnart was the eldest son of the copperplate printer Henri Bonnart, and he had at least ten brothers and sisters. At eighteen he was apprenticed for five years to Jean Ganière, who taught him engraving. He began publishing in the 1660s, alone or with his parents, and engraved portraits of people such as Pope Clement IX. He also worked for the royal household, making architectural plates for Desgodets's book on the antiquities of Rome. He was a French engraver and print publisher.

Hendrik Frederik Sartor worked on contract as a heraldic draughtsman for the Hoge Raad van Adel. His first commission there was the coat of arms for P.M.G. von Fisenne, who was admitted to the Dutch nobility in 1866. His early work resembles that of his predecessor, and his hand is visible in the arms of the two Van der Wyck jonkheers from 1867 and 1868. Besides this he was an arms painter, lithographer and publisher. He had a short training at the Royal Academy in The Hague and kept drawing until his death.

Francis Grant started in law before he turned to painting. Born into a Scottish gentry family at Kilgraston, he went to school at Harrow. At first he painted mainly hunting scenes. He first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1834 and then became a portraitist of high society. His sitters included Queen Victoria and her husband, Lord Palmerston and Benjamin Disraeli. His brother Hope Grant commanded the capture of Peking during the Opium War.

Henri Borremans worked as a lithographer for nearly thirty years. He was the son of a Brussels police commissioner, and little else is known about his life and training, though many of his works survive. His first published work appeared in the French magazine L'Artiste in 1834. With Paul Lauters, Jean-Baptiste Madou and Henri Van der Haert he illustrated a spoof of the French book Les Cent-et-Une Nouvelles. He exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1836.

Joseph Wagner went to Munich at fourteen to train as a painter under Jacopo Amigoni and also learned copper engraving. In 1726 he travelled with Amigoni to Italy and studied further at the Academy of Arts in Bologna. He followed Amigoni to England in 1733 and then went to Paris to study engraving under Laurent Cars. On a second stay in England his first works were portraits of the three daughters of George II. He died in Venice or Munich.

Albertus Steenbergen fell from a table as a baby and stayed disabled all his life, moving on crutches or in a wheelchair. After primary school he worked briefly for a notary. In 1833 he went to Hilversum to study with the painter Jan van Ravenswaay. He mostly painted birds, flowers and insects, in oil and watercolour. In 1836 he moved to Haarlem, where many flower painters lived. Later he turned more and more to writing.

Josef Gerstmeyer was the son of a silversmith. He studied at the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts for fourteen years and exhibited in its shows almost every year. His oils, watercolours and drawings showed views of Vienna and its surroundings and landscapes in Italy and the Austrian mountains, which he visited several times. Some of his works were reproduced as lithographs. He also published a drawing manual with animal studies after Friedrich Gauermann. A lane in Vienna's Aspern district has carried his name since 1956.

Christian Espagne taught himself lithography. He founded the first lithographic institute in Münster around 1820, where Caspar Görke was his pupil. Besides commercial work such as forms, maps and music scores, he made portraits, including about 58 likenesses of the envoys gathered for the Peace of Westphalia, copied from historic portraits in the town halls of Münster and Osnabrück. He was born in Berlin and died in Münster.

Josef Marastoni, born in Venice, learned painting from his father Jakab Marastoni and studied at the Venice art academy from 1850 to 1853. Afterwards he worked in his father's studio in Stuhlweißenburg. From 1868 he lived in Vienna as a member of the Künstlerhaus. His lithographs follow the manner of Josef Kriehuber. He also made etchings. He died in Vienna.

Paul Baudoüin became known above all as a fresco painter. He studied with Charles Gleyre, Jules-Élie Delaunay and Pierre Puvis de Chavannes and entered Puvis's atelier at the École des beaux-arts in 1874. On the advice of the school's director, Castagnary, he learned fresco technique. He married a granddaughter of Jules Michelet, and they had two sons. At the Paris World's Fair he won a gold medal for two decorative works. In 1902 he received a commission for the Maison Hannon in Brussels.

Cornelis Drebbel became a skilled copper engraver and was also interested in alchemy. Born in Alkmaar into an Anabaptist family, he went around 1587 to the Haarlem academy, where his teachers were Hendrik Goltzius, Carel van Mander and Cornelis Corneliszoon. In 1595 he married Goltzius's younger sister Sophia and settled in Alkmaar. They had at least six children, four of whom survived. At first he worked as a painter and cartographer as well as an engraver. He later became an inventor and tutor to the royal children of England.

Frank Johnston studied in Germany from 1904 and returned to Canada in 1907. He later continued at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts under Philip Leslie Hale and Daniel Garber. Back in Canada he worked first as an illustrator at Grip Ltd, where he met future members of the Group of Seven such as Tom Thomson. He showed in the Group's first exhibition in 1920 but soon separated from it, over differences in artistic direction and doubts about commercial success.

Franz Sigrist was the sixth of nine children, born in Breisach on the Rhine. At seventeen he came to Vienna, where in 1744 the imperial academy took him in and he studied with Paul Troger and Jacob van Schuppen. When the academy closed for three years because of money troubles after the Silesian wars, he worked in private studios. It reopened, and in 1749 he was listed as a pupil of the drawing class. He worked as a painter and engraver.

Jean-Jacques Outhwaite was born John James Outhwaite in Shoreditch, London, and became a naturalised Frenchman. He worked as a burin engraver. He married Joséphine Charlotte Dallet in Paris, and they had several children. His son Jean-Louis, a draughtsman, married the daughter of the engraver Émile Thérond in 1871. His daughter Henriette married a Crédit foncier official in 1867. His youngest daughter, Diane Lucie, was a pianist.

René Péan trained under Jules Chéret and made around 150 posters at the Chaix printing works between 1895 and 1913, advertising the theatre, tourism and department stores. His family came from the Sarthe and settled in Paris early in the Second Empire. He entered Chéret's workshop in 1889 as an apprentice lithographer. His colleagues at Chaix included Lucien Lefèvre and Georges Meunier. His posters show smiling, elegant young women or landscapes.

Georg Maria Eckert won a scholarship at eighteen to study painting at the Düsseldorf academy. At twenty he moved to Munich and made study trips to Upper Bavaria, Italy and Switzerland. Back in Düsseldorf he joined Johann Wilhelm Schirmer's landscape class, and he then worked as an art teacher and landscape painter in Heidelberg, where he married in 1858. From 1867 he took up photography and published folders of landscape and architectural photographs. He also built models and collected Baden folk costumes.

Auguste Donnay trained as a craftsman and studied in evening courses at the Liège academy under Adrien De Witte. A scholarship took him to the Académie Julian in Paris in 1885. Puvis de Chavannes influenced him. In 1888 he began his career as an illustrator for Caprice-Revue and La Wallonie. With Armand Rassenfosse and Émile Berchmans he designed posters for the publisher Auguste Bénard. In 1900 he became professor of decorative art at the Liège academy.

Johann Christoph Dietzsch was born in Nuremberg in 1710 into a family of artists. His father Johann Israel and six siblings, among them Barbara Regina, also worked there as draughtsmen and engravers. The family never left Nuremberg, even when offered good positions elsewhere. From 1730 until his death in 1769 he made drawings, watercolours, engravings and gouache paintings. He mainly showed landscapes with rural figures.
